title: After Repair Value (ARV) Explained: Comps and Limits
metaDescription: What after repair value means, how to choose and adjust comps, how ARV ties to your rehab scope, and where the seventy percent rule helps and where it fails.
h1: After Repair Value (ARV): How to Calculate It and Where It Goes Wrong
dek: After repair value is the price a property should sell for once the planned renovation is finished, estimated from recent sales of similar renovated homes nearby. It is only reliable when the comps match the finished house you are actually going to build.
keyTakeaways: ARV is the expected market value of a property after a specific renovation scope is completed, not after a generic or imagined rehab.
Good comps are recent, close, similar in size, age, style, bed and bath count, and finished to the level you plan to deliver.
Adjustments correct for real differences between a comp and your subject property, and every adjustment should be one you can explain.
The seventy percent rule is a screening shortcut for flips, not an underwriting method, and it breaks down in very high and very low price ranges.
ARV and the rehab scope must be built together, because the finish level determines which comps apply.

sections.body:
After repair value, usually shortened to ARV, is the estimated market value of a property once a defined renovation is complete. It answers one question: if this house were finished the way we plan to finish it, what would a typical buyer pay for it, or what would an appraiser say it is worth?

ARV matters to almost every investor strategy. Flippers use it to estimate sale proceeds. BRRRR investors use it to predict the refinance appraisal. Hard money and fix-and-flip lenders use it to size loans, since many lend against a share of the after-repair value rather than the purchase price. Wholesalers use it to price contracts. Even FHA 203(k) borrowers rely on an as-completed appraisal, which is the same concept applied to an owner-occupant.

The important word in the definition is defined. ARV is not the value of the best house on the street. It is the value of this house with this scope. A house with a painted original kitchen and a house with new cabinets and stone counters will have different ARVs, even if everything else is identical. That is why an ARV estimate without a written scope behind it is mostly a guess.

ARV is also an estimate, not a fact. Two careful analysts can land on different numbers for the same property, and the market can move between purchase and sale. The goal is a figure you can defend with evidence and a range that shows how much risk you are carrying.

sections.h2: How do you choose comparable sales?
sections.body:
Comparable sales, or comps, are recently sold properties similar enough to your subject property that their prices tell you what yours should bring. Choosing them well is most of the work in estimating ARV.

The criteria that matter most:
- Recency. Closed sales from the most recent period available carry the most weight. Older sales may need a market-time adjustment and should be used only when recent ones are scarce.
- Proximity. Stay as close as possible, ideally within the same subdivision or the same blocks. Crossing a major road, school boundary, rail line or neighborhood edge can change value more than distance suggests.
- Property type and style. Compare ranches to ranches, two-stories to two-stories, attached to attached. Buyers value these differently.
- Size. Above-grade living area should be close. Finished basement space is usually valued differently from above-grade space.
- Bed and bath count. Matching bedroom count is important, and bathroom count often matters even more.
- Age and construction. Similar era homes share similar systems, layouts and buyer perceptions.
- Lot and site. Lot size, a busy-street location, a backing to commercial use or a view can all move value.
- Condition and finish level. This is the one investors most often get wrong.

Use closed sales as your evidence. Active listings show the competition you will face and pending sales hint at direction, but list prices are asking prices. An appraiser will rely on closed sales, and so should you.

Aim for several strong comps rather than many weak ones. Three to five close matches usually tell you more than a long list of loosely similar houses.

sections.h2: Why finish level is the comp criterion that matters most
sections.body:
The most common ARV mistake is comparing a planned rehab to the most expensive renovated sale in the area. That comp may have had an addition, a gut kitchen with high-end appliances, a finished basement, new windows and a landscaped yard. If your scope does not include those things, it is not your comp.

Think of a neighborhood as having several price tiers among renovated homes. At the top are full renovations with layout changes and high-end finishes. In the middle are solid investor-grade renovations with new kitchens and baths, new flooring and updated systems. Below that are cosmetic refreshes with paint, flooring and fixtures but original kitchens and baths. Then come unrenovated sales, which may be estate sales, investor purchases or homes needing work.

Your job is to identify which tier your scope puts the house in, then use comps from that tier. Read the listing remarks and look at the photos of every comp you use. Note the kitchen, the bathrooms, the flooring, the windows and anything unusual. A comp with a new roof and new mechanicals can support a higher price than a cosmetically identical house with aging systems, because appraisers and buyers both notice.

This is also why it pays to price more than one plan. An estimator can show what a rental-grade version, a standard flip version and a higher-finish version of the same house would cost, and the comps for each tier tell you which version produces the best return. Genstone Construction often prepares multiple ARV plans for exactly that reason. The question is never just what a finish costs, but whether the comps reward it.

No comp is a perfect match, so analysts adjust comp prices to account for differences. The logic is simple: if a comp has something your subject property will not have, subtract its value from the comp price. If the comp lacks something your subject will have, add its value.

Common adjustment categories include:
- Living area, often handled with a value per square foot derived from the local market rather than a citywide average.
- Bedroom and bathroom count, especially a missing full bath.
- Garage, carport or lack of parking.
- Basement finish and basement type.
- Lot size, corner lot, busy road, or backing to non-residential uses.
- Condition and finish level, when you cannot find comps in the same tier.
- Market time, when the comp sold long enough ago that prices have moved.
- Seller concessions, when a comp's price included credits back to the buyer.

Good adjustments are supported by the market itself. One method is paired sales: find two sales that are nearly identical except for one feature, and the price difference suggests the value of that feature. Another is to look at how local appraisers typically handle a given item.

Keep adjustments small and few. If a comp needs heavy adjustments in several categories, it is probably not a good comp. The adjusted prices of your best comps should land in a tight band. When they scatter widely, the spread is telling you the ARV is uncertain, and your offer should reflect that uncertainty rather than the most optimistic comp.

sections.h2: What is the seventy percent rule?
sections.body:
The seventy percent rule is a quick screening formula used by house flippers. It says the most you should pay for a property is seventy percent of its after repair value, minus the estimated cost of repairs. The remaining share of ARV is meant to cover financing, holding costs, closing and selling costs, and profit.

Its value is speed. When you are reviewing many properties, the rule lets you discard deals that clearly do not work before you spend time on a walkthrough or a detailed estimate. It also forces you to account for repairs explicitly rather than folding them into a vague sense of what a property is worth.

The rule is widely repeated, but it was never meant to replace real underwriting. It assumes that selling, carrying and financing costs are a roughly fixed share of the sale price, and that a fixed share of profit is the right target. Neither assumption holds everywhere. The rule also takes both of its inputs as given, so if your ARV is optimistic or your repair estimate is thin, the formula will produce a confident wrong answer.

Use it as a filter, then build a proper deal analysis for any property that passes. That analysis should list the actual purchase closing costs, loan points and interest for the expected hold period, taxes, insurance and utilities while vacant, agent commissions and seller closing costs on the resale, and a contingency reserve. Compare the projected profit against the risk of the specific house rather than against a rule of thumb.

sections.h2: Where the seventy percent rule breaks down
sections.body:
The seventy percent rule works best in the middle of a market, on ordinary houses, with ordinary rehab scopes. It works poorly at the edges.

In lower-priced markets, the fixed costs of a flip such as closing fees, insurance, utilities, permits and a minimum level of rehab do not shrink in proportion to price. The share of ARV they consume is larger, so following the rule can leave too little margin. Many investors in lower-priced areas use a stricter screen or a flat minimum profit target instead.

In higher-priced markets, the rule can be too conservative. The costs of a flip grow more slowly than the sale price, so an investor who insists on the rule may never win a deal that would still be profitable. Competitive buyers in those markets often work from detailed cost models instead.

The rule also fails when the rehab is unusually large or unusually small relative to value. A heavy structural rehab carries more risk and a longer hold, which deserves a larger margin. A light cosmetic refresh may deserve a smaller one.

It does not fit BRRRR or rental strategies at all. Those investors care about whether the refinance appraisal will return their capital and whether the rent supports the new loan, not about resale profit. A BRRRR deal can make sense at a purchase price the seventy percent rule would reject, and the reverse is also true.

Finally, it ignores timing. A market that is softening between purchase and resale can erase the margin the rule assumed.

sections.h2: How ARV and the rehab budget depend on each other
sections.body:
ARV and the rehab budget are not separate calculations. Each one depends on the other, and building them in isolation is how investors end up with a well-researched value for a house they cannot afford to build, or a careful budget for a house the comps will not reward.

The practical sequence looks like this. First, pull comps broadly and sort them into finish tiers. Second, decide which tier the subject property can realistically reach given its layout, size, location and condition. Third, write a scope that delivers that tier and price it line by line. Fourth, check that the scope actually matches the comps you selected, item by item: kitchen level, bath count and finish, flooring, windows, roof and mechanicals. Fifth, if the margin is thin, test a lower or higher tier and see whether the economics improve.

Some improvements carry their weight and some do not. Adding a bathroom where comps show the market strongly prefers more baths may move value considerably. Upgrading to luxury finishes in a neighborhood where every comp has mid-grade finishes usually does not. Systems work such as roofs, electrical and HVAC may not raise the appraisal much on its own, but missing it can lower the price buyers will pay or kill a deal at inspection.

This back-and-forth is the core of what a pre-offer review should do: estimate the repair cost, refine the ARV against the scope, and test whether the numbers still support the offer before money is committed.

sections.h2: ARV for refinance versus ARV for resale
sections.body:
Investors use the same term for two slightly different numbers, and mixing them up causes trouble.

Resale ARV is what you expect a buyer to pay. It reflects buyer emotion, staging, presentation and how many competing listings exist when you go to market. It can sometimes exceed what an appraiser would conclude, particularly when inventory is tight.

Appraised ARV is what a licensed appraiser will conclude for a lender. Appraisers rely on closed sales, apply adjustments according to established methods, and must reconcile their comps into a single opinion of value. They do not credit staging, and they are cautious about stretching beyond the range of the best comps.

For a flip, resale ARV drives profit, but the buyer's appraisal still matters because a low appraisal can force a price reduction or kill a financed sale. For a BRRRR or any refinance, appraised ARV is the only number that matters. If your strategy depends on pulling capital out with a refinance, build your ARV the way an appraiser would: closed sales only, close proximity, matching tier, conservative adjustments.

A useful habit is to estimate both and track the gap. When resale ARV is far above a conservative appraised ARV, the deal depends on market conditions holding. When the two are close, the deal rests on firmer ground.

faqs.q: How do you calculate after repair value?
faqs.a: Start with a written rehab scope so you know what the finished house will be. Then find recent closed sales of similar homes nearby that were finished to the same level, adjust each comp for real differences such as size, bath count, garage and lot, and reconcile the adjusted prices into a single estimate. Weight the closest and most similar comps most heavily. The result is the after repair value, and the spread of the adjusted comps shows how confident you can be in it.

faqs.q: How many comps do I need for an accurate ARV?
faqs.a: Three to five strong comparable sales usually give a reliable estimate, which mirrors how many appraisers approach a residential appraisal. Quality matters more than quantity. A few recent, nearby sales of similar homes renovated to the same level as your planned scope are far more useful than a long list of loosely related sales. If you cannot find enough good comps, treat that as a sign the ARV is uncertain and leave more margin in your offer.

faqs.q: Is the seventy percent rule still useful?
faqs.a: It is useful as a fast screening tool for flips, particularly in mid-priced markets with ordinary rehab scopes. It is not a substitute for a real deal analysis, and it can mislead in low-priced markets where fixed costs take a bigger bite, in high-priced markets where it may be too conservative, and for BRRRR or rental strategies where resale profit is not the goal. Use it to decide which properties deserve a closer look.

faqs.q: Can I use active listings as comps for ARV?
faqs.a: Active listings show what you will be competing against when you sell, so they are worth reviewing, but they are not evidence of value because list prices are only asking prices. Appraisers and lenders rely on closed sales. Pending sales can hint at market direction. Build your ARV from closed sales and use active and pending listings as a reality check on pricing and finish expectations in the neighborhood.

faqs.q: Why did my appraisal come in below my ARV?
faqs.a: The most common causes are comps from a higher finish tier than the finished house, comps that were too far away or too old, heavy adjustments the appraiser did not accept, and a market that shifted between purchase and appraisal. Appraisers also do not credit staging or presentation. If you plan to refinance or sell to a financed buyer, build your ARV the way an appraiser would, using conservative closed sales that match your actual scope.
